title: India Starts Pivoting Away From Russian Oil as New US Sanctions Law Bites; Saudi Restarts East-West Pipeline
subhead: Indian refiners are trimming Russian crude purchases just as a new US law authorizes 100% tariffs on major buyers, while Saudi Arabia restarts its East-West pipeline as the main workaround to the Strait of Hormuz disruption. Oil slid below $100 on Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within a week.

sections.heading: India Eases Off Russian Crude Ahead of New US Sanctions Law
sections.body: India's imports of Russian crude fell 16.5% in August and are expected to decline again in September, according to trade data cited in an OilPrice.com review of Reuters figures — even as Russia remains India's largest supplier. Russian shipments dropped to about 2.1 million barrels per day in August from July's record, with preliminary Kpler data pegging September at 1.9 million bpd. The August decline largely predates the new law, so it is not yet a sanctions retreat; Indian refiners were already shifting barrels as Middle East routes improved, lifting Iraqi purchases roughly 25% to 171,000 bpd. But October and November buying will be the real test: Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Friday, giving Washington authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from qualifying major buyers of Russian energy. India's crude import bill has already jumped 48.4% to $74.8 billion in the April-August period, eroding the savings from discounted barrels, OilPrice.com notes.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now directly targeting the price break that anchored India's Russian oil purchases — the single biggest remaining buyer — threatening to turn a commercial arbitrage into a geopolitical liability just as New Delhi needs stable supply.

sections.heading: Saudi Restarts East-West Pipeline, the Escape Hatch Around Hormuz
sections.body: Saudi Arabia has restarted its East-West oil pipeline, restoring at least some flow through the ~4 million bpd route to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, per Reuters sources reported by OilPrice.com. The pipeline is running at a low rate, with Aramco working toward full capacity and a complete restart still potentially weeks away; one cargo was scheduled to load at Yanbu Tuesday for China. The route had become the kingdom's main workaround after the September 10 drone attack forced its shutdown and pushed Aramco to reroute crude through the Persian Gulf and ship-to-ship transfers near Oman. Traders are already preparing for the related SUMED corridor to Egypt to reopen, moving tankers toward Port Said and Sidi Kerir. The physical market still has plenty of damage to unwind — Saudi flows remain well below normal and diesel stays tight after refinery disruptions in Russia and the Middle East.
sections.whyItMatters: Restoring this inland route reduces Saudi dependence on Hormuz transit — but the slow return and continued tightness show how much resilience the Red Sea corridor has lost to drone strikes, and how fragile the normalization is.

sections.heading: Iran Offers to Reopen Hormuz Within a Week, Oil Breaks Below $100
sections.body: Iran has offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases pressure, including steps toward ending the military blockade of Iranian ports and halting operations in the strait, a senior Iranian official told Japan's Kyodo News, per OilPrice.com. The proposal has been conveyed to Washington and includes resumption of talks aimed at permanently ending hostilities. Brent slipped below $100 a barrel for the first time in a week, trading around $98, with WTI near $91, before prices rebounded later as traders weighed diplomacy against ongoing supply risk. Iran will consult intermediaries during the UN General Assembly in New York this week, but no direct Trump-Pezeshkian meeting is expected. Over the weekend, Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei communicated seven conditions for negotiations, including ending the blockade and releasing frozen assets.
sections.whyItMatters: The seven-day window is a concrete, time-bound negotiating position rather than a vague overture — it tests whether Washington will trade blockade relief for restored flows, and whether either side can afford the optics of appearing to blink first.

sections.heading: Libya's Sharara Field Hit by Armed Group Blockade
sections.body: Crude production at Libya's largest oilfield, Sharara, has slumped after an armed military group closed a valve on the pipeline carrying crude to the Zawiya export port, Libya's National Oil Corporation said, per OilPrice.com's review. Output has fallen from an estimated 340,000 bpd to roughly 120,000 bpd, and NOC warned it may declare force majeure if the closure continues, saying the move would cut state revenue and risk the transport system. The disruption adds another pinch to an already strained global supply picture at a time when Hormuz flows remain uneven and Yanbu exports are only beginning to come back.
sections.whyItMatters: Libya's recurring militia blockades are a reminder that supply fragility is not confined to the Gulf — a 340,000 bpd field offline compounds the tightness and gives the market another reason to keep a risk premium built into prices.

sections.heading: European Industry Feels the Squeeze as UK Gas Prices Force Idling
sections.body: Chemical giant INEOS is idling three plants in Hull, UK — Europe's last remaining world-scale Acetyls units — blaming natural gas prices now 12 times the US level and 8 times China's, per the company's statement and OilPrice.com. With Henry Hub around $2.83 per MMBtu and UK wholesale gas above $23 per MMBtu, chairman Jim Ratcliffe warned Europe is 'losing its last world-scale' acetyls capacity, with replacement supply set to come from the US and China at higher carbon footprints. The plants produce materials for pharmaceuticals, construction, detergents and military explosives.
sections.whyItMatters: Strategic self-sufficiency is eroding in real time: high gas prices are shifting basic industrial production — including defense-critical materials — out of Europe, an economic consequence of the energy squeeze that outlasts any single market move.

bottomLine: Today shows both halves of the supply equation working at once: Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within a week and Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline restart point toward normalization and dragged Brent below $100, while India's quiet pullback from Russian crude, Libya's Sharara blockade, and INEOS idling British plants show how quickly new disruptions and new sanctions dynamics keep the risk premium alive. The watch item is Washington's response to Iran's time-bound offer, and whether October loadings confirm India is really pivoting away from Russian barrels under the threat of the new US tariff authority.
sources: OilPrice.com, Reuters (via OilPrice.com), Kyodo News (via OilPrice.com), Anadolu Agency, Libya National Oil Corporation (via OilPrice.com), INEOS (via OilPrice.com), Kpler (via OilPrice.com)
